names.name: Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls
names.th: ม้วนแผ่นเงินเคเทฟฮินโนม

text.what: Two sheets of silver, tiny, rolled tight, each scratched with a passage of the Priestly Blessing from the Book of Numbers. They were found rolled and had to be opened; the method for doing it without losing them took three years to develop. They hold what may be the oldest surviving text of the Hebrew Bible.
text.story:
Ketef Hinnom is the shoulder of rock where the Valley of Rephaim meets the Valley of Hinnom, on the old road from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, beside St Andrew's Church. Gabriel Barkay reported the first season there in 1975: a salvage excavation on the hill between the church road and the road down into the valley, prompted by a block of stone 2.80 m long lying on the surface, which turned out to be a threshold still in place in a monumental complex. Underneath were rock-cut burial chambers in natural caverns, Iron Age Judahite, of the seventh and sixth centuries BCE.

In 1979 the two silver scrolls came out of one of those chambers. The excavation report describes them as apparently once used as amulets. They are dated to the First Temple period, late seventh to early sixth century BCE, before the Babylonian Exile. They are now in the Israel Museum.

*Inference —* two things about this object are unusual for the atlas at once. It is a written charm that survives from before the tradition it belongs to had a canon to quote from, and it is a charm whose text is not a spell but a blessing. Whether the people who rolled them up would have called them amulets is a question the excavation cannot answer, and the cited report does not claim more than 'apparently'.
text.how: Silver, hammered thin, inscribed, rolled, and worn or carried. How they were suspended is not published in what this project read; what is documented is where they ended up, which is a burial chamber.

text_th.what: แผ่นเงินเล็กจิ๋วสองแผ่น ม้วนไว้แน่น แต่ละแผ่นมีข้อความตอนหนึ่งจากพรของปุโรหิต (Priestly Blessing) ในหนังสือกันดารวิถีขีดเขียนไว้ ทั้งสองแผ่นพบในสภาพม้วนอยู่และต้องคลี่ออก วิธีคลี่โดยไม่ให้แผ่นเงินเสียหายใช้เวลาพัฒนาถึงสามปี ม้วนเงินนี้อาจเป็นข้อความของคัมภีร์ไบเบิลฮีบรูที่เก่าแก่ที่สุดที่ยังหลงเหลืออยู่

dating.period: Iron Age Judah, First Temple period
dating.label: late 7th to early 6th century BCE
dating.note: The cited article gives both 'dated to 600 BC' and 'late 7th to early 6th century BCE'. The years here are that century-span in astronomical form; the tomb complex itself is dated to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

object.made_by: not published in the sources this project read
object.inscription: portions of the Priestly Blessing of Numbers 6:24–26
object.note: No published measurement was read; the article calls them tiny. Worn is given as grave because the findspot is the one placement the excavation establishes.

against.who: the excavation report, which describes the scrolls as apparently once used as amulets; the text on them is a blessing rather than a named harm
against.note: the Priestly Blessing asks that the wearer be blessed and kept; it names no enemy, and this record does not supply one

against.who: the findspot: an Iron Age Judahite burial chamber
against.note: filed from where the object was found, not from anything the object says; the atlas does not know whether they were buried as grave goods or simply worn to the grave

holdings.what: the two silver scrolls, preserved and displayed

kin.as: the commandment that puts the same kind of verses in a box on the body — and the object this one keeps getting read backwards through
the other Jewish text-in-a-container, fixed to a doorpost instead of worn
the written Jewish amulet as a class, of which this is the oldest dated survivor
the tradition of writing a holy text to carry, a thousand years before it had that name
the metal that let a text this small survive two and a half thousand years in a tomb
the practice that is the reason this object exists to be read
the same object in another scripture — a verse, rolled small, worn
scripture in a case at the throat; this is that idea's oldest dated instance in the atlas
the long read about what it means to date an amulet; this one is dated by a tomb, a threshold stone and three years of unrolling

object.note: script is given as palaeo-Hebrew, which is the First Temple period script; the cited article names the period, not the script, so treat that field as unverified

text.how.note: reasoned from the object's material and findspot; no manufacturing account was read
